Transport and Merge: Cross-Architecture Merging for Large Language Models

Use optimal-transport correspondences between attention and MLP activations to transfer knowledge across heterogeneous language-model architectures.

Cui Chenhang

February 5, 2026 ·ICML 2026 ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF ·Code
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

Transport and Merge uses optimal transport over activation relationships to establish correspondences between heterogeneous language models. These correspondences guide layer and feature alignment, making cross-architecture weight fusion possible. A small shared input set supplies the evidence needed to connect the two models.

The work evaluates knowledge transfer in low-resource language and domain settings, and explores residual-frozen adaptation after fusion. It separates the problem of finding a functional correspondence from the subsequent problem of integrating the transferred representation.

OTCross-neuron correspondence
CrossHeterogeneous model fusion
SmallShared-input alignment set

Transferring knowledge across architectures begins with finding which internal computations correspond.

Why this matters

Conventional merging often assumes compatible architectures. That assumption limits transfer from high-resource source models to heterogeneous targets with limited task or language data.

How it works

  1. Collect activations from source and target models on a small set of shared inputs.
  2. Solve optimal transport to establish correspondences between heterogeneous neuronal representations.
  3. Use the resulting transport plans to guide direct weight-space fusion.

What the study finds

Experiments across low-resource languages and specialized domains report consistent improvements over the corresponding target models. The transfer uses a small input set to infer the cross-model correspondence.

What this means

This frames model merging as a problem of translation between internal coordinate systems. Architecture can obscure correspondence even when two models contain related computations; activation relationships provide an empirical bridge across that boundary.

The useful outcome is reusable knowledge under limited adaptation data. Future progress depends on identifying when transport plans preserve function, how shared-input coverage affects the mapping, and whether gains survive beyond the domains that supplied the correspondence evidence.
